entry.dc:title: Optimal mining of a stratiform phosphate field
entry.dc:creator: Mehrez A.
entry.dc:description: An optimal control model is developed to determine optimal surface mining operations of a phosphate field. This field1806 1040 contains both a bottom layer and a top layer of phosphates. The deeper the digging, the more phosphates will be exploited but the higher will be the cost per ton. If the bottom layer is not exploited, it will be lost to future production. The methods of Optimal Control Theory are applied and produce expressions which can be evaluated for the optimal scheduling around the phosphate field. © 1984.

entry.dc:title: GROUND CONTROL.
entry.dc:creator: Rajaram V.
entry.dc:description: Recognition of rock mechanics as a practical tool for ground control in surface and underground mines was well established in 1983. Research by the US Bureau of Mines, Office of Surface Mining, and universities across the US was reported in several symposia and publications. Practical applications of ground control techniques were reported at SME Annual and Fall Meetings. Highlights of accomplishments reported are summarized.

entry.dc:title: Simulation of a small surface coal operator
entry.dc:creator: Kinek P.A.
entry.dc:description: A simulation model has been constructed as a framework to study the consequences of government regulations, and the de lays inherent in these regulations, on the functional areas of small surface coal operators. This paper specifically looks at the ef fect of the Surface Mining and Reclamation Act promulgated by Congress in 1977. The act has altered basic operating deci sions of coal operators in land management. Some of the critical changes the regulations have brought about are lengthy and costly permit preparation procedures, lengthy local and state review of permits and lands, increased bond fees, and costly reclamation requirements. The proposed model is useful as a quick turn-around policy analysis tool. © 1984, Sage Publications. All rights reserved.
entry.authkeywords: government regulation | policy-making | surface coal operator | system dynamics

entry.dc:title: WIDE RANGE OF DIESEL POWER OFFERED.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: A table summarizes the main engines available from U. S. manufacturers for surface mining equipment such as dozers, wheel loaders, scrapers, excavators, drills, cranes, compressors and off-highway haulers. Many of the models have multiple ratings because of accessories such as turbocharging and aftercooling.

entry.dc:title: Properties of minesoil reclaimed for forest land use.
entry.dc:creator: Bussler B.H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Soil Science Society of America Journal
entry.dc:description: Physical and chemical properties of minesoil reclaimed for forest land use in SW Indiana were evaluated to determine suitability for reforestation. Properties of reconstructed minesoil and unmined reference soils were compared. Soil types on the reference area were primarly Ava (Typic Fragiudalf) and Parke (Typic Hapludalf) silt loams and were similar to soils on the mineland prior to excavation. Both the reclaimed mineland site and reference site supported mixed upland hardwood trees and shrub vegetation prior to surface mining. Chemical properties of minesoil were similar to or more favorable for plant growth than unmined reference soils. However, physical properties in the rooting zone were less favorable in minesoil than reference soils.-from Authors

entry.dc:title: New Data Relative to Sulfide Mineralization in the Badeanca Valley-Leaota Massif Basin.
entry.dc:creator: Pop G.
entry.dc:description: A survey was performed during the 1977-1982 period which has revealed the extent of the mineralization indices in the entire basin. This includes data pertinent to the metamorphical formation of the Leaota Series, and surface mining. Work done in this tectonic area confirms the occurrence of Cu, Co, Ni, Pb and Zn.

entry.dc:title: EXAMPLES OF CURRENT SURFACE MINING RESEARCH: OPERATIONAL AND POTENTIAL.
entry.dc:creator: Treuhaft M.
entry.dc:description: Expectations for coal in the early to mid-1970s prompted the government and industry to pursue research and development programs to increase underground and surface mining coal productivity and net coal recovery. Three presented in this paper are: extended depth augering for trench-strip applications; high recovery auger heads for enhanced recovery; and variable wall mining in low cover longwalls. Conceptual development is examined, prototype testing is discussed, and potential operations are considered.

entry.dc:title: EVALUATION OF A DRILLING SYSTEM FOR A LARGE OPEN-CAST-MINE - A DISCUSSION.
entry.dc:creator: Nanda N.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: The success of surface mining operations depends upon the ability to break rock. The parameters and steps needed for appropriate selection of the drilling equipment are given. It is shown that for a large open-cast mine the modern large diameter drill is capable of drilling both rotary and percussion. This type of machine is favored in many operations as it can handle both hard and soft material by changing to percussion or rotary drilling. The key to selection of a particular equipment is its flexibility in operation.

entry.dc:title: SOIL-DEPTH REQUIREMENTS TO REESTABLISH PERENNIAL GRASSES ON SURFACE-MINED AREAS IN THE NORTHERN GREAT PLAINS.
entry.dc:creator: Barth R.
entry.dc:description: Because of the importance of soil in the reclamation of land disturbed by surface mining and the high costs associated with the salvage and eventual return of soil during the reclamation process, a study was initiated to quantify soil-depth requirements for revegetation of surface-mined lands in the Northern Great Plains. Production responses of cool-season perennial grasses were dependent on spoil traits, and this study identified four spoil types: generic, sodic, acid, and soil-like. Depth of soil required to maximize forage production averaged 50 cm for generic spoil, 71 cm for sodic spoil, indeterminate for acid spoil, and 0 cm for soil-like spoil.

entry.dc:title: TRENDS IN SURFACE MINING AND QUARRYING.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Cost-conscious operators are looking for mining equipment and ideas that can boost productivity in hard times. Few and forunate are the mineral industry sectors which have been able to expand production and generate good profits during the past years. Severe cost savings have almost invariably had to be made; these have been achieved by stopping unprofitable activities and delaying the replacement of plant and machinery. Nevertheless, spurred by the hard facts of the economic situation, new ideas abound and methods which have been accepted in the past as the best are under searching review and are being vigorously challenged.

entry.dc:title: Wetlands and coal surface mining in Western Kentucky - A regional impact assessment
entry.dc:creator: Mitsch W.J.
entry.dc:description: A wetland atlas (Mitsch etal. 1983) was developed for a 3960 km<sup>2</sup> region of the Western Coalfield in Kentucky to inventory the wetlands there and to present a regional assessment of coal surface mining. Both the methodology and the results of the atlas are presented as they relate to wetland management. The atlas was designed to present the location, type, and extent of wetlands as well as useful environmental and ecological information for both wetland managers and coal mine operators. The study identified 460 km<sup>2</sup> of wetlands with about 84 percent as broad-leaved deciduous forested wetlands. There were also 5.6 km<sup>2</sup> of needle-leaved deciduous wetlands (bald cypress swamps) and 24.3 km<sup>2</sup> of persistent emergent wetlands, scrub-shrub wetlands, and dead forested wetlands. Surface mines were also identified from aerial photography for the atlas and were often shown to be contiguous with existing wetlands. Data on hydrology, water chemistry, and fish and wildlife resources were gathered from several sources to supplement the mapping and inventory results. The complete inventory showed that surface mining had several impacts on wetlands, including 1) direct removal, 2) acid drainage, 3) sedimentation, and 4) altered hydroperiod. © 1983 Society of Wetland Scientists.

entry.dc:title: Revegetation methods for arid areas, revised.
entry.dc:creator: Willis C.
entry.dc:description: Reviews reclamation practices currently used by the Arizona Department of Transportation, and methods recommended for revegetation of surface mining operations.-from STAR, 22(14), 1984

entry.dc:title: BIOLOGICAL & HYDROLOGICAL IMPACTS OF SURFACE MINING FOR FEDERAL MINERALS IN THE TYRO CREEK WATERSHED, ALABAMA: PREMINING - AQUATIC BASELINE INFORMATION.
entry.dc:creator: Harris S.
entry.dc:description: This report is a compilation of water quality, hydrological, and biological information from Tyro Creek watershed (Tuscaloosa County, Alabama) prior to the initiation of surface mining for Federal coal in the Little Tyro Creek lease tract. This information will be utilized to provide a preliminary data base by which the hydrological and aquatic biological effects of surface mining and subsequent reclamation in the wateshed can be assessed. The information gathered in this study can also serve as an aquatic assessment model for coal development in similar small stream watersheds in the Warrior coal field.

entry.dc:title: SYNTHETIC CRUDE FROM OIL SANDS.
entry.dc:creator: de Malherbe R.
entry.prism:publicationName: Fortschritt Berichte Der VDI Zeitschriften Reihe 3 Verfahrenstechnik
entry.dc:description: Oil sands and heavy oils have the present advantage of being among the most accessable of unconventional resources. Furthermore, recovery technology is established and commercially demonstrated in Canada, where these synfuels presently supply 10 percent of the nation's oil needs. The Canadian experience with processing oil sand and heavy oils is of considerable interest to the rest of the world. In this study, a basic overview of recovering and upgrading hydrocarbons from oils sands and heavy oils is presented. The methods discussed include surface mining of oil sands, the extraction of bitumen from tar sands, in situ recovery of hydrocarbons from heavy oil deposits, the upgrading of raw bitumen, and the direct conversion of oil sand feed to synthetic crude.

entry.dc:title: GEOLOGICAL AND GEOCHEMICAL CONTROLS ON THE CHEMICAL EVOLUTION OF SUBSURFACE WATER IN UNDISTURBED AND SURFACE LANDSCAPES IN WESTERN NORTH DAKOTA.
entry.dc:creator: Groenewold G.H.
entry.prism:publicationName: Report of Investigation North Dakota Geological Survey
entry.dc:description: Previous studies of several surface coal-mining sites in western North Dakota have resulted in the development of a hydrogeochemical model which accounts for the observed chemical characteristics of subsurface water in undisturbed settings. The major purposes of this study were to refine the hydrogeochemical model with particular emphasis on the sulfur cycle, and to determine the applicability of the model to postmining (spoils) landscapes. From the study the authors conclude that the hydrochemical model is equally applicable to undisturbed and spoils landscapes and that the major species of concern in this region are sodium and sulfate. Negative hydrogeochemical impacts resulting from surface mining in the Northern Great Plains will include increased mineralization of groundwater, sodic and salt effects on plants and increased mineralization of surface waters.

entry.dc:title: ADDITION OF COAL MINING REGULATIONS TO THE COMPUTER-AIDED ENVIRONMENTAL LEGISLATIVE DATA SYSTEM (CELDS).
entry.dc:creator: Webster R.D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Special Report US Army Construction Engineering Research Laboratory
entry.dc:description: Deartment of Energy (DOE)-specific regulations on mining have been added to the Computer-Aided Environmental Legislative Data System (CELDS), an online, interactive database developed by the U. S. Army Construction Engineering Research Laboratory (CERL). CELDS indexes and abstracts environmental regulations of the Federal government and the 50 states. Included now are coal mining regulations for the Federal government and those states having Department of Interior approval for their mining programs. The coal miing regulations cover Federal Regulatory programs for surface mining and underground mining of coal on Federal, Indian, and private lands. A draft thesaurus of mining terms has been developed, This thesaurus, which will be merged into the existng CELDS thesaurus, will be used to index CELDS records which cover coal mining regulations. The thesaurus terms cover both coal miing technology and environmental impacts of coal mining.

entry.dc:title: ECONOMIC EVALUATION OF BOREHOLE AND CONVENTIONAL MINING SYSTEMS IN PHOSPHATE DEPOSITS.
entry.dc:creator: Hrabik J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Information Circular United States Bureau of Mines
entry.dc:description: An economic comparison of the borehole mining system with conventional dragline and bucket wheel excavator mining systems was completed at various mining depths and production rates. Discounted cash flow analyses based on derived capital and operating costs were used to generate rates of return and product prices. Borehole mining was more economical where overburden thickness was 150 ft or greater; at 50- and 100-ft thicknesses, conventional surface mining was more economical. Borehole mining is environmentally more desirable.

entry.dc:title: Reclamation of deep mine refuse banks with municipal sewage sludge
entry.dc:creator: Seaker E.M.
entry.dc:description: Municipal sludge was applied on a deep mine anthracite refuse bank at rates of 80 and 108 dry Mg/ha to facilitate vegetation establishment. A monitoring system was installed to determine the effects of the sludge applications on the quality and growth of the vegetative cover, chemical properties of the soil, and chemical and bacteriological quality of the groundwater. Data collected over a 5-year period indicate that the addition of sludge improved the physical and chemical condition of the black, highly acidic refuse material and promoted establishment and continued growth of a complete vegetative cover. Sludge applications resulted in slight increases in some trace metal concentrations in the surface soil and in the vegetation. However, soil concentrations were within the normal range found in U.S. soils. Vegetation foliar trace metal concentrations were well below plant tolerance levels and no phytotoxicity symptoms were ever observed. In general, the sludge applications had no significant adverse effect on the chemical or bacteriological quality of groundwater. The results indicate that single applications of stabilized municipal sludge, applied at rates up to 108 dry Mg/ha with lime, can be used in an environmentally safe manner to revegetate coal refuse banks in the Appalachian mining region, with a cover that is self-maintaining for the 5-year period mandated under the federal Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. © 1983, Sage Publications. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Federally required restoration of surface-mined property: impasse between the coal industry and the environmentally concerned ( USA).
entry.dc:creator: Rasnic C.
entry.dc:description: The US Federal Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 is supposed to guarantee post excavation restoration. Reviews the practical problems encountered in enforcing this legislation and the differences in viewpoint separating the extractors and local environmental groups.-T.O'Riordan

entry.dc:title: The costs and benefits of federal regulation of coal strip mining.
entry.dc:creator: Kalt J.P.
entry.dc:description: This study amounts to a quantitative cost-benefit analysis of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (SMCRA). Incidence and welfare effects of SMCRA are developed within the context of a multi-sector model of the US coal industry. It appears that, on net, the national economic costs of SMCRA outweight the benefits, albeit by a narrow margin. SMCRA appears to produce substantial improvements in resource allocation in certain regions of the country. Still, SMCRA is far from a first best policy. The 'real story' of SMCRA probably lies in the wealth transfers it produces. These are found to be large and, most likely, regressive. -from Author

entry.dc:title: Improving aquatic wildlife habitat through coal surface mining in the Plains.
entry.dc:creator: Parr D.
entry.dc:description: If regraded spoil depressions and sediment settling basins have a reliable supply of water, reclamation permits may be obtained to manage these areas as aquatic habitat after the mining finishes. In many cases, slurry ponds may be reclaimed as wetlands by covering acid-bearing zones with earth fill, then establishing suitable aquatic plant communities in the various resulting water depths. Waterfowl and sport fishes are being managed successfully in reclaimed impoundments at a number of Mid-western mines.-from Authors

entry.dc:title: Energy use and production: Agriculture and coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Land G.W.
entry.dc:description: Many people are concerned that surface mining for coal and other mineral resources is destroying substantial amounts of farmland and should, therefore, be prohibited or severely restrained. Questions are also raised concerning the net amount of energy that surface-mining for coal yields. Use of land to produce energy crops is urged as a preferable alternative to surface mining. This paper examines the idea and presents comparisons of the true energy cost of farming and mining as ways to produce energy for our use. © 1983.

entry.dc:title: USE OF LABORATORY METHODS TO QUANTIFY DUST SUPPRESSANT EFFECTIVENESS.
entry.dc:creator: Lane D.D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: Three types of dust suppressants used in the surface mining industry to control fugitive particulate emissions from unpaved roads were tested for cohesive strength and resistance to reduced effectiveness by large water additions. Each product tested varied in cohesive strength with a range of 34-300 kPa (5-44 psi). Strength depends on aggregate moisture content and the means by which the sample is dried. Large water additions to the road surface after initial suppressant application can produce undesirable results.

entry.dc:title: APPLICATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL GEOLOGY TO LIGNITE MINING IN TEXAS.
entry.dc:creator: Henry C.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: Environmental geologic maps of the Wilcox and Jackson-Yegua lignite belts of the Texas Coastal Plain delineate land areas on the basis of their natural characteristics. Criteria used to define map units include substrate, soil, topography, geologic process, vegetation, and land use. The maps are useful in planning and reclamation of lignite mines and in meeting the requirements of state and federal surface mining laws. Specific applications include identification of land capability, recharge areas and geometry of aquifers, flood-prone areas, areas that may qualify for prime farmland status, and other areas sensitive to lignite mining.

entry.dc:title: Effects of surface mining on the microbiology of a prairie site in Alberta, Canada
entry.dc:creator: Visser S.
